title: Boumediene v. Bush
lead: Foreign nationals held at Guantanamo challenged years of executive detention after Congress withdrew habeas jurisdiction. The Supreme Court held that the Suspension Clause reached the base and that the restricted statutory substitute did not provide adequate review, while leaving detention authority and individual release for later proceedings.

actors.name: Boumediene and consolidated Al Odah petitioners
Justice Souter
actors.role: Concurring Justice joined by Ginsburg and Breyer

actors.name: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Scalia

proceedings: Following statutory changes and earlier Supreme Court decisions, the D.C. Circuit dismissed for want of habeas jurisdiction. On June 12, 2008, the Supreme Court reversed five to four and directed return to the district court for habeas proceedings.
limits: The Court invalidated Military Commissions Act section 7’s habeas withdrawal, not the review tribunals themselves. It did not decide their due-process adequacy, the substantive detention standard, conditions claims, innocence, or entitlement to release.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Capture and status review left the detentions contested
sections.cue: Introduce the prisoners and the executive process.
paragraphs: The Executive relied on the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force to detain foreign nationals at Guantanamo Bay. Some had been apprehended in Afghanistan, others as far away as Bosnia or Gambia. None was a citizen of a country then at war with the United States, and each denied al Qaeda or Taliban membership.

After Hamdi, the Supreme Court decision addressing wartime detention of a citizen, the Defense Department created Combatant Status Review Tribunals to determine enemy-combatant status under its definition. Each petitioner received an adverse determination. They contested those determinations; the Supreme Court did not adopt enemy-combatant status as an established factual premise.

sections.title: Congress changed the review path during the litigation
paragraphs: Habeas actions began in February 2002. The district court and D.C. Circuit initially dismissed because Guantanamo was outside United States sovereignty. In Rasul in 2004, the Supreme Court held statutory habeas jurisdiction extended to the base, leaving the constitutional question open. Back below, Judge Leon dismissed one group for lack of enforceable rights; Judge Green held the Fifth Amendment protected the other group.

During those appeals, Congress enacted the Detainee Treatment Act in 2005, withdrawing habeas jurisdiction for Guantanamo aliens and giving the D.C. Circuit exclusive review of final tribunal determinations. Hamdan held that withdrawal inapplicable to pending cases. Congress responded in the 2006 Military Commissions Act by expressly extending the new withdrawal to pending cases. The D.C. Circuit held jurisdiction removed and the Suspension Clause inapplicable, making the substitute’s adequacy unnecessary to decide.

Before the Supreme Court, petitioners argued the new effective-date language covered only other detention actions, not habeas. Justice Kennedy rejected that distinction. The phrase other action linked the provisions, habeas related to detention, and the response to Hamdan confirmed the withdrawal’s breadth. Congress had supplied the required clarity; statutory avoidance could not preserve jurisdiction by contradicting that choice. The constitutional question had to be faced.

sections.title: History informed the constitutional inquiry without resolving it mechanically
sections.cue: Explain the structural protection and geographic problem.
paragraphs: Kennedy treated habeas both as an individual safeguard against unlawful imprisonment and a check requiring the Executive to justify confinement. Its development through common-law struggles, the Petition of Right, and the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 explained the Constitution’s restricted suspension power. Separation of powers protected persons, not citizens alone.

Founding-era practice did not conclusively answer Guantanamo’s unusual situation. Alien status was not categorically disqualifying, but prisoner-of-war cases and writs involving exempt jurisdictions, India, Scotland, Hanover, Ireland, and Canada were imperfect analogies. English courts in India did not establish what courts in England could accomplish abroad. Competing legal systems and enforceability could explain geographic limits. The incomplete history’s lack of an exact precedent proved neither side’s case.

Cuba retained formal sovereignty under the lease and treaties, a political determination the Court accepted. Yet United States jurisdiction and control were complete and uninterrupted, amounting to practical sovereignty. The political branches could not retain total control while arranging formal sovereignty to switch constitutional constraints off. The Insular Cases and Reid, precedents considering constitutional application in differing territories and circumstances, supported attention to local conditions and feasible alternatives. Kennedy read Eisentrager’s postwar Germany setting and military obstacles as integral rather than treating its territorial language as exclusively controlling.

sections.title: Control and practical conditions favored habeas at the base
sections.cue: Apply the framework and distinguish prior military review.
paragraphs: The framework considered at least citizenship and status, including the process establishing status; capture and detention locations; and practical obstacles to judicial review. Unlike Eisentrager’s prisoners, these petitioners disputed status without a rigorous military trial providing lawyers, evidence, and cross-examination. Tribunal personal representatives were expressly neither lawyers nor advocates, government evidence enjoyed a presumption of validity, and detainees could present only reasonably available evidence.

Unlike temporary, shared Allied occupation in Germany, control of Guantanamo was absolute and indefinite. No Cuban court competed, and no credible showing established that habeas would compromise the base’s mission. Ordinary resource costs did not outweigh those features. Active combat or serious conflict with host-government authority might present a different case. The Suspension Clause had full effect at Guantanamo. The Military Commissions Act neither purported to suspend formally nor was defended as a formal suspension.

sections.title: The statutory substitute lacked necessary judicial powers
sections.cue: Explain why the Court reached adequacy and the governing minimum.
paragraphs: Although the D.C. Circuit had not decided adequacy, the Supreme Court addressed it because years without meaningful oversight and the separation-of-powers stakes made the cases exceptional. The parties had briefed it, and parallel Bismullah decisions supplied the circuit’s understanding of the review record.

Hayman and Swain, precedents approving relocated collateral review, preserved broad powers and savings clauses for ineffective substitutes. Here Congress deliberately narrowed review, omitted a savings clause, and assigned exclusive appellate review without district-court factfinding transfer. Text, structure, history, and comparison with statutory habeas showed that this was not ordinary habeas under another name.

Adequate review had to give a meaningful chance to show detention rested on mistaken law and permit conditional release when necessary. Further requirements depended on context. Executive detention required meaningful examination of both factual cause and executive authority, especially without a prior fair judicial hearing. Kennedy analogized that relationship to procedural rigor in Mathews v. Eldridge without making a due-process holding.

Limited evidence access, no counsel, hearsay, and practical inability to confront accusations created serious error risks, especially for confinement potentially lasting a generation. Hamdi did not resolve this Suspension Clause question: statutory habeas remained available there and its tribunal discussion came from a plurality. Even assuming these tribunals satisfied due process, independent habeas protection remained. The reviewing court needed power to assess evidentiary sufficiency, correct error, consider omitted exculpatory material, and provide appropriate relief, including release when necessary. Neither a criminal trial nor a precise government evidentiary burden was prescribed.

sections.title: Later-available evidence exposed a concrete gap
sections.cue: Explain why favorable statutory assumptions still failed.
paragraphs: The Court assumed for argument that statutory review could imply release authority, permit challenges to the military-force authorization, and correct factual findings. It also assumed Bismullah properly included government information reasonably available when the tribunal sat. Even then, evidence becoming available afterward remained excluded.

Petitioner Nechla had asked his tribunal to contact an employer supporting his denial of al Qaeda affiliation. The tribunal found the witness relevant but unavailable; counsel now represented that the witness could be heard. The statutory review still excluded that evidence. Asking the Deputy Secretary to convene another tribunal was insufficient because it was discretionary and a refusal was not a reviewable final tribunal determination.

Constitutional avoidance could not rewrite the scheme into the extensive habeas review Congress meant to remove. Nor did the Court promise that fixing only later evidence would suffice or demand that every substitute duplicate statutory habeas. Taken together, the restrictions were facially inadequate, making Military Commissions Act section 7 unconstitutional. The Detainee Treatment Act and tribunal system themselves remained intact.

sections.title: The petitioners could proceed without further exhaustion
sections.cue: State the remand and matters preserved.
paragraphs: Some petitioners had been held six years, and statutory applications had languished more than two years without merits decisions. They need not exhaust that route before district-court habeas. This did not require immediate judicial intervention on capture: absent undue delay, the Executive ordinarily should have reasonable time for status assessment, with courts accommodating genuine exigency and intelligence interests.

The Court suggested venue mechanisms directing cases to the District of Columbia and judicial protection of intelligence sources and methods. Detailed evidence and counsel-access questions, substantive detention law, and confinement-condition claims remained unresolved. It reversed the D.C. Circuit and directed remand to the district court, ordering no release and finding no petitioner innocent.

sections.title: The separate opinions disputed both reach and adequacy
sections.cue: Give the complete division of views.
paragraphs: Justice Souter, joined by Ginsburg and Breyer, joined Kennedy fully and emphasized that Rasul’s historical reasoning had already alerted the government to habeas’s relevance. Four years since Rasul and six years of some detentions made claims of judicial haste unconvincing.

Chief Justice Roberts, joined by Scalia, Thomas, and Alito, would dismiss because the statutory system adequately protected whatever rights existed. He wanted exhaustion and actual circuit review before constitutional reach was decided. He viewed tribunals as a first collateral-review tier modeled on Hamdi, followed by Article III scrutiny. Representatives, evidence and witnesses, appellate counsel, and factual and legal review provided adequate military process. Remand for new evidence, regulatory reconsideration, annual review, and implied release authority answered the majority; he disputed that refusal to reconvene was unreviewable. He objected to hypothetical defects and predicted district-court litigation would delay relief and resemble the displaced system.

Justice Scalia, joined by the same three Justices and also joining Roberts, independently would affirm because the Clause did not protect aliens abroad. He viewed Eisentrager’s territorial rule as controlling and accused the majority of evading stare decisis. The Insular Cases concerned sovereign territory, while Reid concerned citizens. His history confined the English writ to Crown dominions, distinguishing restrictions on sending prisoners away and correcting his prior inclusion of Scotland. Historical ambiguity, he argued, favored Congress rather than enlargement through structural abstractions. His warnings about military burdens and dangerous mistaken releases were dissenting predictions, not findings about these petitioners.
Kennedy’s opinion for Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer prevailed five to four on June 12, 2008.
